Some people exist just to be consolation prizes. Edward Stewart of New York is no exception to that rule. Edward is not an inspiring liberal icon. In fact, while he claims he's a liberal, his observed politics are left-of-center. Because he's only liberal-coded and not a radical liberal, that's why he was chosen to be your running mate.

Representing the 28th District of New York, Edward has gotten the hang of saying liberal-leaning rhetoric without actually implementing liberal style governance. If New Yorkers from his liberal district kept electing him based on 'liberal charm', then, why wouldn't the outraged liberals in the national Democratic Party believe in Edward too?

The Democratic Party doesn't need to go in a leftward shift at all. Just because a moderate such as yourself won the primary doesn't mean that the Democratic Party needs to overtly throw the liberals out. No, the Democrats have someone who is quite good at 'conciliatory liberal politics'. He seems nice and inoffensive, just like yourself...

For whatever reason, this man considers himself a part of the Democratic Party. Senator Douglas Brown is a terrible choice to be your running mate if you're intending to run a liberal style campaign. Senator Brown sits solidly on the Establishment wing and is rumored to have been a favorite with the party's bosses. The running mate slot was clearly stolen from Senator Murphy Alston Young.

Hailing from the once-Democratic state of Arkansas, Senator Brown has made a name for himself as being a conservative Democrat. 'A yellow dog Democrat', if you will. He say he's only supporting the 'Democratic Party' because that's 'what the South used to do'. If he bothered to read the room, he would probably be a Republican.

For all intents and purposes, this man is what faux philosophal thinkers may call 'the anti-thesis' to the liberal Democratic platform. However, maybe a blantantly bad reading of Hegelian Dialetics will work out well for the Party? Your liberal thesis and the conservative Democrat anti-thesis might be able to produce a synthesis?

A Natural Compromise

Now the fact of the matter is that, in the Democratic Party’s recent history, we have never really planned to run a conservative Democrat like Senator Douglas Brown. His running mate, Franklin Howe, was also chosen to emphasize Senator Brown’s conservative Democrat tendencies. I was expecting a moderate to win the nomination and, therefore, win the election. However, compromising to stop the liberals was necessary, even if that meant that Senator Brown and Representative Howe had to become the Democratic nominee.

The Democratic Party wouldn’t be able to win the 2076 election if the liberals were able to get their way. Still, the truth is that Senator Douglas Brown was ‘an unknown variable’ so to speak. There was no way to know exactly whether or not the American electorate was going to approve Senator Brown’s candidacy. I recognize that choosing Brown made the Democratic Party practically a copy of the Republican Party but with a blue outward appearance. I have no regrets whatsoever to that characterization of the Democratic Party.

To prevent the un-American liberals from becoming the Democratic Party’s ultimate choices for President of the United States of America was something that I, as Chairman, had to do. Senator Brown and Representative Howe may not have been able to win the 2076 election against President Dirk Edwin Rodney and Vice President Alfred Tabor Richardson. However, the Democratic Party has managed to prevent un-American radical liberal ideologies from taking over the Party. I have seen how the left wing of the Democratic Party thinks about the rest of the Party. I made sure that the left wing would not force the Democratic Party to accept radically left-wing political agendas.

I know where I stand on the issue. My position as Chairman of the Democratic Party lets me know who is in the right and who is in the wrong. Without a doubt, at this point in time, the leftists were always going to be wrong. They were never going to be able understand what the Democratic Party is actually like. Senator Brown ‘did his best’ against the incumbent President Rodney. How could I or anyone else in the Democratic Party know that Senator Brown might lose the election?


Samuel Ulf Nordeck

Chairman of the Democratic Party

The Wheels on the Bus

What a fine morning. I've been forced to wake up at 4:30 a.m. in the morning on this Saturday, October 23, 2077. The Los Angeles Metropolitan Transit Authority has 'let me choose' a Saturday shift. All the while, the wife gets to sleep in just because her factory work schedule has a more predictable work schedule than mine. Oh, of course, she tells me that ‘it’s a job, Edgar. The house, little Ashley, and little Tommy, will be alright…’ Thanks so much Cecilia.

The still-dark hours at home go by quickly. Prepare myself, clothing, and all of that that other self-maintenance. Eat some Pork n’ Beans from the fridge and throw the can into the trashcan. Get into one of the two Corvegas that our household owns. Keep the thought in the back of my mind that these cars are nickeling and diming us on top of the fact we have an apartment to rent. Cecilia and I can’t pay off both of these cars thanks to the high APR and interest payments. Fantastic stuff.

Go to the station and reach there at 4:45 a.m. in the morning. Sun isn’t even up yet and I’m already up! The military ought to wake up at this time: 4:00 a.m and 5:00 a.m.? Why should I care about this time?

Check in and realize that my routes are a few morning commuter routes with a normal route on top for good measure. The only consolation is that I’ll get to go home in the afternoon today. Bus driving is a terrible job. Those with seniority get first picks over what routes and times they want to drive. They even get to be selective about which days they want as their rest days.

'Course they always get to take the day off on Saturday and Sunday considering how everyone else below the seniors are forced to take rest days that land on weekdays. Whatever routes that the seniors didn’t choose are considered scraps that are left for those more junior them. Unfortunately for me, I’m one of those juniors. Doubly unfortunately, I’m doing a Saturday shift. Fine, fine. FINE.

I go to the bus that I’m going to be driving this morning. I do all the tests that I have to do to make sure the bus is in working order. Air Brake tests, air governor cut in and out, applied air leakage test, low air warning tests, spring brake test, air compressor build up rate checking, rear door interlock checking, parking brake test, and service brake test. Procedure is procedure. If the bus passes everything, like it should, my day is going to be routinely irritating. If the bus fails a test, my day gets an unexpected additional irritation. 'Fortunately', the bus passes all the tests. The time is already 5:17 a.m. No sunlight, of course. I put on the radio to give a sense of atmosphere for myself and future passengers who will take the bus.

I drive this large vehicle out of the depot. The traffic in the pre-dawn morning of California isn’t that bad. Fuel shouldn’t be a probably consideration. The thing runs on nuclear power like a lot of other vehicles anyways.

First things first, to the first stop in West Hollywood. This first route should take me from 5:33 a.m. to 6:21 a.m. from stop to stop to stop. Getting a bunch of people from Point A to Point B as a job.

The passengers, maybe the majority of them, are very much not bothersome. They want to get from here to there. They neither say thank you nor do they want to cause a scene. I ignore them. The ones that spoil my day are the ones that are rude. They think they know it all and won’t hesitate to correct you. ‘You were late, you were early, you were too slow, you’re a stupid idiot, you’re a clueless bus driver, you didn’t wait 10 more seconds, you need to do this or that even if it isn’t in the regulations’. I’m not beholden to them, but, I can’t argue with them. They will not apologize nor own up to their mistakes. Their stubbornness prevents them from understanding reason or pleas for empathy. All I can do is say polite nothingness that mask my sheer indignation. Justified indignation. I am being degraded by those who, if they were truly rich, would degrade somebody else instead of me. They could get their own personal chauffeur, but, no, they’re poor and so, they degrade me instead. Just a normal bus driver who lets them off the bus without a fuss when they have reached their destination. I’m not getting thanked for this job.

Stop to stop. Stop to stop. I finish my first route at 6:22 a.m. It is what it is in my books. I get going once again. I reach my next stop at 6:28 a.m. Traffic is starting to get worse, as usual. As the day goes on, the traffic will have to get worse. I reach my next stop at 6:32 a.m. I then move on and get to the next stop at 6:38 a.m. The sun is beginning to shine. The sun often starts rising at around this time in Los Angeles anyways.

Loud blaring sirens start to ring out in Los Angeles. I continue driving, just like many other Los Angelinos. Some people have decided to park on the side of the road to consider why there are sirens.

The radio blares a beep. Another beep. Static. Beep, beep, beep. Static. Beep, beep, beep. Static. There’s an announcement. There’s a nuclear war. I make a decision that would get me fired as I pull the bus over to the side of the road. I check the time: 6:42 a.m. I slump down in the driver’s seat as I tune out the commotion in the back. I sigh, “Finally…” Everyone else panics as I choose to not restore order in the bus. I open the bus door. It would not matter to me in the end. If they want to run, they can run.

I think to Cecilia, Ashley, and Tommy. Probably still in bed. Probably not going to feel a thing.

Dad’s not going to be home with them in bed…

Schadenfreude

Samuel Ulf Nordeck

Chairman of the Democratic Party

The Wheels on the Bus

Got to wake up at 4:30 a.m. in the morning on this Saturday, October 23, 2077. Forced to work a Saturday shift for the Los Angeles Metropolitan Transit Authority. All the while, the wife gets to sleep in considering her factory work schedule has a more predictable work schedule than mine. She says that ‘it’s a job, Edgar. The house, little Ashley, and little Tommy, will be alright…’ Thanks so much Cecilia.

Prepare myself, clothing, and all of that. Eat some Pork n’ Beans from the fridge and throw the can into the trashcan. Get into one of the two Corvegas that our household owns. Both these cars are nickeling and diming us on top of the fact we have an apartment to rent. Cecilia and I can’t pay off both of these cars thanks to the high APR and interest payments. Fantastic.

Go to the station and reach there at 4:45 a.m. in the morning. Sun isn’t even up yet and I’m already up! The military ought to wake up at this time: 4:00 a.m and 5:00 a.m.? Why should I care about this time?

Check in and realize that my routes are a few morning commuter routes with a normal route on top for good measure. The only consolation is that I’ll get to go home in the afternoon today. Bus driving is a terrible job. Those with seniority get first picks over what routes and times they want to drive. They even get to be selective about which days they want as their rest days.

'Course it’s always Saturday and Sunday considering how everyone else below the seniors are forced to take rest days that land on weekdays. Whatever routes that the seniors didn’t choose are considered scraps that are left for those more junior them. Unfortunately for me, I’m one of those juniors. Doubly unfortunately, I’m doing a Saturday shift. Fine, fine. FINE.

I go to the bus that I’m going to be driving this morning. I do all the tests that I have to do to make sure the bus is in working order. Air Brake tests, air governor cut in and out, applied air leakage test, low air warning tests, spring brake test, air compressor build up rate checking, rear door interlock checking, parking brake test, and service brake test. Procedure is procedure. If the bus passes everything, like it should, my day is going to be routinely irritating. If the bus fails a test, my day would get an unexpected additional irritation. The bus passes all the tests. The time is already 5:17 a.m. No sunlight, of course. I put on the radio to give a sense of atmosphere for myself and future passengers who will take the bus.

I drive this large vehicle out of the depot. The traffic in the pre-dawn morning of California isn’t that bad. Fuel shouldn’t be a probably consideration. The thing runs on nuclear power like a lot of other vehicles anyways. On my way to the first stop in West Hollywood. This first route should take me from 5:33 a.m. to 6:21 a.m. from stop to stop to stop. Getting a bunch of people from Point A to Point B as a job.

The passengers, maybe the majority of them, are very much not bothersome. They want to get from here to there. They neither say thank you nor do they want to cause a scene. I ignore them. The ones that spoil my day are the ones that are rude. They think they know it all and won’t hesitate to correct you. ‘You were late, you were early, you were too slow, you’re a stupid idiot, you’re a clueless bus driver, you didn’t wait 10 more seconds, you need to do this or that even if it isn’t in the regulations’. I’m not beholden to them, but, I can’t argue with them. They will not apologize nor own up to their mistakes. Their stubbornness prevents them from understanding reason or pleas for empathy. All I can do is say polite nothingness that mask my sheer indignation that I am being degraded by those who, if they were truly rich, would degrade somebody else instead of me. They could get their own personal chauffeur, but, no, they’re poor and so, they degrade me instead. Just a normal bus driver who lets them off the bus without a fuss when they have reached their destination. I’m not getting thanked for this job.

Stop to stop. Stop to stop. I finish my first route at 6:22 a.m. It is what it is in my books. I get going once again. I reach my next stop at 6:28 a.m. Traffic is starting to get worse, as usual. As the day goes on, the traffic will have to get worse. I reach my next stop at 6:32 a.m. I then move on and get to the next stop at 6:38 a.m. The sun is beginning to shine. The sun often starts rising at around this time in Los Angeles. Loud blaring sirens start to ring out in Los Angeles. I continue driving, just like many other Los Angelinos. Some people have decided to park on the side of the road to consider why there are sirens.

The radio blares a beep. Another beep. Static. Beep, beep, beep. Static. Beep, beep, beep. Static. There’s an announcement. There’s a nuclear war. I make a decision that would get me fired as I pull the bus over to the side of the road. I check the time: 6:42 a.m. I slump down in the driver’s seat as I tune out the commotion in the back. I sigh, “Finally…” Everyone else panics as I choose to not restore order in the bus. I open the bus door. It would not matter to me in the end. If they want to run, they can run.

I think to Cecilia, Ashley, and Tommy. Probably still in bed. Probably not going to feel a thing.

Dad’s not going to be home with them in bed…

February 26th, 2077

I thought that I’d get to see Sean fail at triage with the Corporal while the Corpsman is busy dealing with the hundreds of other casualties. Or, maybe, I’d have to finally see Ken stop joking about arbitrary death and accept his death if he was downed in the field. Or maybe, Corporal Fryar would finally get screwed his head the right way. All they can do is just transfer me to Headquarters & Service Company and give me a desk job at the rear. The enlisted Jarhead who just lost his job is probably incensed. I would be too. The green weenie gets what it wants, especially when ‘your Dad’ is the President who controls it to screw over other enlisted.

Why must it be this way? Did Dad really have to win the Presidential election? I thought he’d let me stay in the field and not have to get any paperwork to remove me from the front. Got a degree, but not eligible for OCS. Average PFT and CFT and OSO didn’t notice me does that. I’m not cut out for ‘sir’ style leadership, whether it be in politics or in the Corps, but I sure love being with the plainly downright rude Ken, the hidden joker Sean, and the unshakably stern Corporal Fryar.

I don’t deserve to get less of the suck. I deserve to get more of it. At least I would be in the suck with the ones that I love. It’s not right to be singled out.

Corporal Fryar wasn’t any less nice. Called me a weasel for trying to escape the frontline and leaving Ken and Sean to die without me giving the fire team scouting heads-up. Kept having to say ‘Yes Corporal’. Next-up, our 'ruthless' squad-leader. Sergeant Hernandez was quite calm and gave me a brief run-down before handing me off to Staff Sergeant Campbell. Staff Sergeant Campbell had no two ways about it. I’ve been handed a ticket to be an POG. Yes, all of 3/9 and the entirety of the Marine Corps knows about it now. No, I’m getting no sympathy.

The paperwork came from above ‘prepared for me immediately from the day your father became President’. Seemed to be gesturing to some puppetting thing... ‘Yes Staff Sergeant’. Report to Gunnery Sergeant Knight of 2nd Platoon. Meet someone who I have probably never needed to meet one-on-one who seemed fed up. Get wrangled through a whole line of admin stuff ‘specially prepared’. Just even more false niceness that I know real Marines don’t bother with until I wound up where I was supposed to be. Didn’t matter if they were in the field or not.

All I know is that I am just a junior enlisted in a field of officers and enlisted who have their own community back here. They don’t know me and what the real 3/9 is feeling down there. I don’t care about what they think of me.

Mom and Dad probably wanted me to be safe. I get it. But, I’m safe when I’m with Sean, Ken, and Corporal Robin Fryar, in the field. Not when I’m in the presence of Marine officers like Captain Martin Ultrecht of S4 Logistics. Wouldn’t ever want him to be in the command of a real Company, like that of Kilo Company. Just endless nitpicking that Ken and Sean wouldn't ever believe happens back here. This form, that form, any MOS can do your job so do it. And so, there's fear, sir.

It’s safer here than it is out there. Don’t they know that I can always get shelled by one of the inland Chinese artillery or shat on by a Chinese flyboy? They can always do that if they wanted to. It’s not the worst of worlds. But, it’s not where you’ll be able to call some idiot your best friend without finding out that your ‘new best friend’ is just a Blue Falcon at the end of the day. It’s just the way things are.

Lance Corporal Nicholas Neville – S-4 Logistics, Headquarters and Service Company, 3rd Battalion, 9th Marines, 3rd Marine Division

The Best of America

If one were to look out at San Diego right now, you would see nothing but radioactive ash. America is in ash. California is my home, and yet, I am perhaps one of the last remaining survivors who hailed from California. From where I’m standing, I can’t really see San Diego. This is my life now, which is to be stuck on this Poseidon Oil Rig that is 175 miles off the Coast of California. The Enclave calls this place their base of operations. The Oil Rig is the home of what is left of America’s old world. I doubt that anybody else is still alive on the mainland. Perhaps some may still be alive in those badly designed vaults, but, aside from that, probably no one else has survived the Great War. ‘October 23, 2077, is a date which will live in infamy’.

I should be proud that I am alive and still able to serve as President. I was the first San Diegan Governor of California. I am now the first San Diegan President of the United States of America. Just because I had to strike a bargain to be initiated into the Enclave is not a bad deal in the end. I had told them that if I was able to win the Presidency of the United States, the powers-that-be should let me become an Enclave member. They have kept their deal. By their own words, they call me one of the best Presidents in the history of the United States. ‘I have made no mistakes during my Presidency’. I am happy that I get along well with them.

From what I have been told by those in the Enclave, my rise to become President Neville of the United States hinged on the fact that President Rodney was seemingly far too unpopular with the American public. It was apparently quite fortunate that the other side of the uniparty had chosen a moderate to become the foil to President Dirk Edwin Rodney. If the Democrats had chosen someone like Young, so the Enclave said, well, the Enclave could always just ‘kick his crutches right out from under him.’ Such a metaphor sounds quite harsh to someone who is just a principled man. Still, I cannot complain because I find the people of the Enclave to truly represent the best wishes of America. They are good people. They should have rescued Rodney and Young and some other noteworthy Americans too, but, well, I don’t want to make the people of the Enclave too angry. It’s better to live in harmony with one another on this Oil Rig. That just makes life more bearable.

Whereas the American bureaucracy was vast and redundant in many places, the Enclave has effectively learned how to ‘right-size’ the American government. In the Enclave, we have achieved a more democratic society where every single American is allowed to vote for the President of the United States. Before October 23, 2077, the ordinary, lukewarm inhabitants of the United States of America could not be trusted to vote directly for the President of the United States. Those inhabitants would have chosen someone radical like Young. That was why the Electoral College existed as an institution to ensure that the right people would vote for the right candidates. After October 23, 2077, there only remains Americans who are of the fittest constitution and smartest minds. It would be unethical to deny voting rights to such worthy American citizens.

That is why the Enclave is a democratic society. By popular vote of the best in America, America can choose the most able-bodied President, Vice President, Congresspeople, and judiciaries to guide America. The most able-bodied are held accountable to the fact that there exist punishments, both according to the law of the land but also extra-judicially, for disobedience to the will of the Enclave. Given how the Enclave is made up of what appears to be hardliners, I doubt there is any need to enforce any punishments. As President, I am expected to lead the nation while Congress and the Judiciary are by my side to focus on other tasks on my behalf.

I find that the people of the Enclave are quite nice people who seem to be enthusiastic about seeing someone like myself talk to them and relate to them. They tell me about how President Rodney ‘seemed so distant, so quiet, and so, overall unlikeable’. They find it to be a ‘no-brainer’ for America to elect me. I apparently don’t judge nor do I try to be so harsh to people. ‘That is why you are an effective leader compared to President Rodney’. Perhaps? This is a job, but, I still have to deal with people. If people are on my side and I am on their side, we can work to bettering America.

The Oil Rig is nice. My family is alive and well. I always feared that, perhaps, my little Marine, my Nick, might die in China. I feared that maybe, I would outlive Clementine or Helen.

Those fears have dissipated. Now, my family is safe. The Enclave truly protected the ones that I care about.

The Enclave pulled Nick to the rear lines in China. They then forcefully removed Nick from China and made sure he would stand guard as part of a ‘secret Marine unit’ to guard the Poseidon Oil Rig. When the time would come for me to arrive on the Oil Rig, Nick would be there to greet me when the time came for me to arrive on the Oil Rig. He doesn’t like being a ‘Marine’ amongst ‘Army dogs’, but, really, I can’t give him a life as a Marine. His Marine buddies are probably already dead in China.

Clementine… She always wanted to get away from California and, maybe, find something better in Ohio. She worked her way up from being but a lowly factory worker to that of a factory manager. The government stepped in to offer her a job as a worker on the Oil Rig. She wouldn’t accept on her own volition, but, the Enclave exerted institutional pressure on her superiors and Chryslus Defense to force her to accept new employment or be terminated with a bogus firing. As such, she acquiesced and accepted the new job. Now, Clementine is here with Helen and I on the Oil Rig. Clementine hates being here, but, I wouldn’t want her to be forced to die in the nuclear apocalypse that killed off Chryslus Defense.

It is good to be President. Helen and I were flown to the Enclave Oil Rig just before the bombs fell. Vice President Stewart and his family managed to reach the Oil Rig right after my Vertibird landed.

I am content with my life. I was told to be a man who could govern effectively. I have served my part well. I would like to continue serving America. The Enclave seems to respect me. My family is by my side. I do wonder how America will rebuild itself given how the fittest of America are all that is left of the old world. The new world needs to be built under my watchful oversight…

June 4th, 2077.

They say that the enemy can slit your throat if you don’t keep duty. Doesn’t matter if it’s the sweltering heat of the Chinese sun or the cold of the Chinese night. It’s the story that all the NCOs say. Especially to me, the one that often gets duty. Lance Corporal Kenneth Briggs jokes that you can apparently get executed if you fall asleep on duty. ‘It’s in the regs! You read the regs right? They said back in Korea/Vietnam/2066 Alaska’…. Yeah, keep lugging around the Pig. You wouldn’t want to stand at duty with it. You don’t even need to care about the ammo either. That’s what Lance Corporal Sean Davis does for you. At least he doesn’t complain even if he lovingly hates your guts, Ken. Wish Sean’d pull his weight with duty, though.

Not a single one of us enlisted Devils read those regs. Not a single one of us. So what if the regs say this or that? None of us want to get chewed out on the frontline by Corporal Robin Fryar, that E-4 slimeball who’s always on a power trip. Probably was abandoned as child and thought the Corps would give him a family. For what it’s worth, better to be a lance coolie than to deal with the upper NCOs and SNCOs all the time, like having to deal with our often terse but rumored ice-cold Sergeant Hernandez. Or that supposedly dreadful Staff Sergeant Campbell. Terrible NCOs and SNCOs all around 3/9; still the best that we’ve gotten in the Corps. We’d prefer to listen to Sean impersonate Corporal Fryar than to listen to the real Corporal Fryar. Though, Sean wouldn’t make a good NCO or SNCO. Neither would Ken. It’s why we’re all stuck as non-rate lance coolies.

‘Tragic’ he would always say. Somehow, 3/9 always gets the hardest fighting without any of the glory. Some place known as Baishan Village where there were a bunch of those Chinese. Stop the Chinese. Don’t know whether they’re going to advance or retreat. Just stop ‘em from attacking us ‘on the flank’. It’s my job to alert the rest of the fireteam. And then, we have contact. And then, we hopefully win without breaking our streak of not dying.

‘Tragic’, but what’s a Devil got to do? We’re not one of those dogs or POGs. Being a rifleman’s all right to me. ‘Every Marine a Rifleman’. Every Marine not dead if he’s got Phantom flyboys and indirect fire support called in.

At least at the front, you don’t have MPs constantly finding infractions to ding you for stupid nonsense. MPs at the front get our respect. Corpsmen too. Nobody disrespects Doc. Nobody. Get shot with us and you’re honorarily like us. A real honorary grunt. But, those MPs? Tell them to hang themselves. We haven’t done anything wrong. You haven’t seen the front. Stop trying to make us hate you.

Corporal keeps getting us in danger, and yet, we’re still a happy dysfunctional family of screwups that sticks together. Other fireteams keep getting chewed through and, yet, we haven’t lost anyone yet. Gotta respect him. Wouldn’t want to lose anyone in the fire team now. Maybe later, as in never, but not now.

“We must push the Chinese out of their stupid homeland! Out to the sea!” or something according to the order that flows down the line. How close are we even to Beijing? Probably not that far! Haven’t been seeing the power armored tin men walk by in a long while. Must be because they’re heading north or something. All I know is that as long as none of us get ‘medically separated’ from our brothers or buried out here in China without our brothers, we’ll get home and, maybe, just maybe, try to put these things behind us. If, though.

Lance Corporal Nicholas Neville – 1st Fireteam, 2nd Squad, 2nd Platoon, Kilo Company, 3rd Battalion, 9th Marines, 3rd Marine Division

Working For the Office

The electoral victory of President George Oliver Neville was not an expected outcome. The Democratic leftist base had expected for a leftist champion to emerge from the Convention’s battleground as the true Democratic nominee for President of the United States of America. Nevertheless, defying the doomsaying of the liberal and leftist base, the Democratic ticket of Neville and Stewart were able to take back the White House from President Dirk Edwin Rodney. The liberals and leftists had theorized and protested openly: Only a leftist could win the 2076 election. America was supposedly in dire need of seeing a leftist Democratic President win the 2076 election. Those false prophecies of the cynical and pessimistic liberals, progressive, and radicals had come to pass. There was good reason to be suspicious of the high and mighty claims of the left wing of the Democratic Party. Those high and mighty claims were laid to rest with President George Oliver Neville’s victory in 2076.

The Mundanity of Eternity

The East always rises earlier than the West. I like living in Fairfield. The town is nice. My state is the state of Connecticut. The houses are nice. They also think that I dress kind of funny and tease me for it. Well, I think that they stink. How about that?!? Huh?

I’m all alone at this park.

The sirens are still blaring.

Maybe I should go back home? Won’t Mama and Papa feel worried? Maybe I should…

Maybe, I’ll head home now…

It's getting bright.

Commanding The Assemblyline

Alright, so, I'm now one of the many supervisors at the Cleveland Tank Factory in Cleveland, Ohio. This seems strange to me. One moment, I thought California was dull. Probably still dull even to this day. Then, I leave to Ohio, which is far away from California. Ohio is cheaper than California too. I was a factory worker. And now, the job description changes, but the workload doesn’t get easier. I don’t need to do as much manual labor, but, the work is managerial and based on dealing with people.

Supervising the 50-or-so people who actually do the final quality control is a doozey. I always thought that the previous supervisor, Ms. Hutchinson, was being extremely picky on all sorts of stuff. Clearly, now I see how demanding this supervisor role is. The pay is better, but, I don’t feel fully qualified to be a supervisor. I’ve been working here since when my younger brother Nicholas left to join the Marines and when Dad left the California Governorship. That was 2074. 3 years and I’m already at a supervisor role? That’s not supposed to happen so quickly!

Ms. Hutchinson has become one of the higher-level managers at the Cleveland Tank Factory. I guess she just got sick and tired of being stuck in such a ‘boring role’ as she says. Surprisingly, she’s not as nitpicky as she usually was when she was in my current spot. She’s stern. What type of manager isn’t stern? She also doesn’t intrude too much on my work. That’s something strange. I feel, overall, happier here. The work is less quality control and more-so about managing the people who do the quality control.

Now, I don’t really want to admit it. Ok, fine, I guess I’ll admit it anyways. (It's the truth, so, I can just write it out. Who's going to care besides me?) The quality control where I just trusted the intuition of Suzie and John isn’t something that the regulations call 'acceptable'. Nor was I supposed to ignore my fellow employees when they’re slacking off. Unfortunately, that does mean that I have to keep telling the people who are under my supervision that they have to follow the safety regulations. They have to inspect the tanks carefully. It’s mostly my fault, which has made their lives just a bit harder, but, then again, there’s also Ms. Hutchinson above me. So, I guess I have to do that. The union keeps trying to 'persuade' me to lower my standards. I keep having to talk to Ms. Hutchinson about this. She doesn't seem too pleased about my escalating to her.

Meanwhile, Suzie, John, Lily, Ashley, Charlie, and the 45 other people in my department aren't happy. I get what they're saying. I was once in their shoes before. Still, the work is supposedly getting easier 'or so the people who are experts in this field' say. We now have more robots to make sure people don't get hurt. The robots do the job quickly too. The factory has a lot of people. Fortunately for the people still working here, the union has tried to protect the people from being laid off. The tanks are still getting made. The tanks keep rolling along. Quality control is somewhat better than before? I can see that people try to follow the safety and quality regulations. 'By observable output, errors are down 19.3%, the time to produce a tank from start to finish has decreased by 8.5%, downtime has been reduced by 20.4%.' The company must be so thrilled that they get to produce more tanks at a faster rate and a lower cost.

I try to make sure that I listen to my 'subordinates'. I would prefer to call them my 'former coworkers'. Can't do that because of how a supervisor 'has to conduct themselves in a manner befitting that of a supervisor'. Nevertheless, I feel that people are in despair and apathetic about the work. They seem to be grateful to have a job, but, they're concerned about Chryslus Defense perhaps just laying them off in the future. I can't guarantee that they have a job, so, I try to tell them to focus on the job right now. They don't like to hear that. I'm sorry that I can't do anything to help them.

I think about my younger brother Nick from time to time. Nick in the Marine Corps and fighting in China. He's probably still impulsive like always, maybe? He's probably become a bit more arrogant, perhaps? He doesn't talk about whether he's had to become a leader like me. He doesn't really have any leadership skills. I hope he isn't dead. The letters sent by him from China seem to get fewer and fewer. Or maybe they were lost by the military? But what would Dad think? Mom? No, just, focus on something else...

What's the point of these T-95 tanks anyways? I told Ms. Hutchinson about this. She said she would follow up with an answer. She never did. I don't want to ask a second time. These so-called 'Behemoth' tanks. Surely, America doesn't have enough fuel for them? Nor enough spare parts? How are we even solvent? Aren't we supposed to be losing money?

I'm not paid to do upper-level managerial work. Ms. Hutchinson isn't either. The people who work on the line with the robots matter more than me. I should be down there with them. They wouldn't need to see me become somewhat harsh, I think? I'm sorry about that. A supervisor shouldn't need to be so harsh like Ms. Hutchinson...

Clementine Neville

Cleveland, Ohio

July 7th, 2077.

A Date of Eternal Weekend

On the morning of Saturday, October 23, 2077, Americans from the East to the West were either in bed or preparing to relax in their Saturday weekend. With the regular week over, everything was going to turn out alright. A family in San Diego, California, were waiting to celebrate the birthday of Mr. Jason Fleming, their dad. Mrs. Haley Fleming was already out to prepare breakfast for her three little kids, Harold, Helen, and Heidi. Dad was still asleep. He was always so tired after his long 5-day-shift. The kids are still in bed. No worries, Uncle Patrick and Aunt Vicki were going to attend tonight's birthday party at 5:00 p.m. Mrs. Fleming knew that this Saturday would be a real treat for Mr. Fleming.

Mrs. Fleming was always going to be an early bird. 6:00 a.m. on the West Coast on this special Saturday was just fine with her. Normally, she would still be sleeping until 8:30 a.m., but, today’s the big day. Just prepare some regular eggs and ham for the special Dad of today. The kids only needed to have some cereal and milk ready. That would do. She could do with a quick bite to eat. An apple is fine enough. She ought to be heading out to do the errands for tonight’s 5:00 p.m. party. If anything were to happen, Jason could look after the kids. After all, it’s only 6:37 a.m. If she were to take the car, it would only take her about 5 minutes to get to the nearest grocery shop. But, the car might be low on fuel. She can just take a walk instead. The grocery store doesn’t officially open until 7:30 a.m. Or, she could go to one of those fancy grocery stores that open at 8:00 and 9:00 a.m. Something so quaint, and, yet, it requires so much of her thinking power. It’s only a once-in-a-lifetime 56th birthday party, isn’t it?

There’s some sirens blaring.

That’s concerning.

She looks outside to see the earliest of birds still going about their day.

Don’t they get it? The sirens are unmistakable.

She hurries to wake the kids. The door opens with ease.

6:42 a.m.

“Kids! Wake up!”

They complain and want to stay in bed. It’s just pure panic. Fine.

She hurries to the master bedroom.

She prepares to open the door.

The door creaks open.

It never opens fully…

October 10th, 2077

Did our luck run out? No, my fireteam is known for being lucky. Seeing how long we’ve been together, with us being cut out to start to be better than the Marine Raiders, we’re not meant to die. Our streak can’t be broken. Marines don’t die.

The scent is what we have to deal with. ‘Embrace the suck.’

Ken is invincible. Death’s reserved for others. His Pig’s a beast that is meant to kill the enemy. Rip ‘em to shreds. That’s why he’s laying still. Exhausted. On top of his M60 in this fighting hole of his there. Bleeding out from that brain of his. Helmet punctured by a round. Uniform and vest caked with mud and sweat. Flies.

And Sean. Sean’s just out to get the ammunition. Hasn’t returned. The First trusts him with our lives. If we don’t have ammo, we’re dead. I’ve got ammo for my rifle. So, I’m not dead. Drained, maybe a little rattled by a blast. But, still combat-effective!

We’re not surrounded. No, the Chinese think they could win. Attacked us ferociously... Marines don’t lose. 3/9’s never combat ineffective. Aren’t we near the capital of Beijing soon? Gaowanzhen, perhaps. Right, Corporal Fryar. Last thing I was doing was tending to him. Before, well. A concussion? Knocked out?

He was with me, right?

Slumped down. Stinks. Flies. A blast from something or too. Uniform and vest’s ripped at the belly. Guts and more guts. Extraordinarily still. Where’s the Corpsman? Hold on.

Airway check? Yeah, no air flow. Nope. No pulse. Not going to be fighting at this point.

Should I look up? We were…

Yeah, attacked. Night-time. A desperate bid to hold us off from their capital. We were about to give them what for.

Is that groaning? Sounds like it. It’s either a Marine or one of those Chinese.

No, don’t look up.

Do they see me? Can’t risk popping my head out and encountering one of their ‘human waves’ again…

What’s a single Marine against a horde of them though? Is it smart to stand up now? Mission is to hold this position and wait for reinforcements.

Bodies all around. Chinese. Marines. Was 3/9 lucky? Where’s our reinforcements?

Radio check. Let’s see here.

Got nothing. Maybe adjust frequency…

Still nothing.

Maybe see if the Corporal’s radio works? Frequency check.

No.

Alright. Fine.

Bold. Stand up.

Visual contact.

They’re wearing green. But the enemy does so too.

They look human. Yeah, but all of them are human.

“HEY! ID YOURSELF!”

No response.

“HEY! HEY! FRIENDLY?!? MARINE!”

No, just…

Duck, duck, duck.

A ruse?

Alright, steady…

Grenades, got none.

Weapon check. Magazine inserted. Round in the chamber. Bolt forward. Ejection port cover closed. Weapon on semi-automatic. R91’s ready to fire.

They’re getting closer. Closer.

Throw a grenade down here. I dare you. Come on. Kill me then.

English, isn’t it?

“Sergeant Hall, bunch of bodies here.” That’s one.

Move your fire team up, Corporal Hannigan. Swap out with Corporal Martinez's fire team. Corporal Fernandez's fire team is lagging behind. Rest of the platoon and company are behind us. Lucky you.” That’s two.

“Second fire team is preparing to take point, Sergeant!” That’s three.

Stand up. “DON’T SHOOT. DON’T SHOOT! MARINE!”

“WHAT UNIT, MARINE?!?”

“Lance Corporal Nicholas Neville, 3/9.”

“3/9? Corporal Martinez, 2/8. Seem to be in a rough spot right now, Lance Corporal.”

“Sorry Corporal, but where were you?”

“You were supposed to wait for us! You should be thankful that your and our organic fire support ensured that the Chinese didn’t overrun the entire sector. And, by the way, watch your tone, Lance Corporal. Just because we’re in a combat zone doesn’t mean you don’t show respect.”

The Sergeant’s approaching. Shut myself up. Alright.

“Apologies Corporal.”

“Acknowledged.” ‘Least the Corporal’s not holding any grudges.

“Corporal Hannigan! Perimeter! Secure it!”

“Aye aye, Sergeant! Stevens, Booker, set up fire and assist there! Garret, picket!”

“Aye aye Corporal.” They all say…

Alright, steady...

“Marine, I am going to ask you once: Why didn’t you ID yourself? We repeated it thrice through the radio. What’s your problem?”

“Sergeant, my radio wasn’t working.”

“You could’ve gotten yourself killed! What then?”

“Yes Sergeant. My mistake, Sergeant.”

The Sergeant turns to the other Corporal.

“Martinez, get your Marines to help secure the perimeter. We’re waiting on the rest of the squad, platoon, and company to catch up. The Lieutenant might come up soon…”

“Aye aye Sergeant.”

His attention’s on me again…

“SITREP. Now.”

“October 10th, 2077… Beijing time is 0500? I think because the last time it was around 2300. We were supposed to have been holding Gaowanzhen, which is nearby to a river… Erh… Well, we also defended the position, expected to get some reinforcements before we’re destroyed. Last thing we needed more ammo and medical supplies because of the casualties and how heavy the resistance was. They could have overrun us and all of that, and, casualties is… well, Kilo Company is mostly KIA, WIA, or MIA. Got attacked heavily during the night. Yes, attacked.“

“From which direction? Bearings?”

“North, over that river, Sergeant. Maybe a hundred or so? Bearings, erh… let me che-“

“Where’s your CO? Platoon sergeant? SNCO?”

“Respectfully, Sergeant, I don’t know? But, erh, my Corporal’s been waiting for a Corpsman.”

Some of the Marines look down at where I’m pointing.

They already understand.

“Let me get this straight, you DON’T KNOW WHERE YOUR COMMAND IS? AND KILO COMPANY IS EITHER KIA, MIA, OR WIA?!?”

“Yes Sergeant.”

“Listen, 2/8 is here to relieve your sorry hide. We’ve got some T95s from the 2nd Tank Battalion. Your case, which is beyond a doubt, awful, is something that the Lieutenant and the rest of the officers have to deal with. We’re meant to be advancing right now.”

“Yes Sergeant.”

“Right, are you aware of anyone else who ISN’T mincemeat right now?”

Dear Mom and Dad,

Hope you’re still doing well in California. I had it in the back of mind that I gotta tell you how things are over here. Yesterday, the boys and I saw a raccoon dog. Love,

Nick

The Mundanity of Eternity

The East always rises earlier than the West. I like living in Fairfield. The town is nice. My state is the state of Connecticut. The houses are nice. It doesn’t make sense why Papa and Mama are still in bed. It’s already 9:00 a.m. and I’m hungry. I know, I know, but, it’s just so fun to go outside and take a look at all the stuff. Yesterday, Mrs. Atkinson taught the class about ducks and pigeons and all that. I love the 1st grade so much. There’s even a park near my house known as Veres Park Playground. Sure, people say that it smells, but, I don’t really care! All the kids like to play there. My favorite thing about the playground are the slides. Going down the slides are so fun and wee! So fun. Looking at the clock again, I see it’s only 9:30 a.m. I check on Mama and Papa. Still sleeping. I can just go out for 30 minutes and head back home just as they start to wake up. They’re tired from going to work all-week!

I decide to go out to that park because I like going up the thing. Then, I go down the slide. Then I keep going up and down until I get bored. Then, I do something else! Like looking for birds! Birds go chirp, chirp, chirp. No one’s around really. Sure, there’s Mrs. Arnold and her three kids, Alan, Kyle, and Norman. They’re kind of older than me, so I don’t play with them. They also think that I dress kind of funny and tease me for it. Well, I think that they stink. How about that?!? Huh?

Sadly, I didn’t bring a watch. There’s also some sirens blaring in the distance. They make such a loud noise and it’s not nice that I have to listen to them. Mrs. Arnold and her kids shuffle away. The park is all to myself now. I see some people in the distance who try to run away from something. Grown ups aren’t afraid though! They’re like very much more fearless than me. When I grow up, I want to be somebody tough and mean. That way, Alan, Kyle, and Norman… They can know that sure, I dress funny, but, I’m bigger, meaner, and badder than them. Don’t tease me!

I’m all alone at this park.

The sirens are still blaring.

Maybe I should go back home? Won’t Mama and Papa feel worried? Maybe I should…

Maybe, I’ll head home now…

It's getting bright.

Nicholas probably thinks he’s so tough being a Marine in China. My younger brother's so goofy. I even got a job working at one of those factories owned by Chryslus Defense, that large government-funded subsidiary of Chryslus Motors. The factory is known for producing those T-95 medium tanks. 'Behemoths' I often muse. People on the floor like to call it that. Sorry, I don’t talk much about tanks. The T-95 doesn't have a real name either. I work in a factory that builds them. I don’t drive them. I certainly don't feel like I would ever want to crew one of them. I think that the American military may not have enough fuel to supply the tanks, but, if Chryslus Defense wants to keep manufacturing the tanks, I can’t say anything really. The whole factory floor has a lot of these robots going around. They do a lot of the menial jobs: Riveting, coating, assembly, all sorts of things that a person used to do. I feel as though everything flows along swimmingly. Management talks about how it is now very safe to be a worker at the big defense factories. Seeing things from that point of view, maybe it really is safer compared to the past. People seem to get hurt less. People who have a job here also feel right at home too.

Still, the job isn't defined by just supervising robots all day. We have less workers on hand, but, more 'skilled, managerial workers' at that. You still have to work as a big team. Still have to be friendly and willing to help out. If you can brighten someone's day, that's even better. They'll feel much happier. We'll also all feel much happier.

The assembly line keeps rolling down. All the pieces get put together. My job's just final quality control. Most tanks look fine enough. Some need to get off the line and sent back down for say Suzie or John to take a harder look at. They just have that sense of intuition. Never do I ever want to bring things up to the supervisor, Ms. Hutchinson though. Whenever she comes down from her office, she is trying to find a fault to deflect responsibility. If she actually did come down here more to see how hard we've been working, maybe, just maybe then, she would stop trying to critique us so often. I see our form. Our form is good enough. Overall, the job at the factory is good enough. I see that I am more fortunate than other men and women. They should feel upset about not being able to find a job. Automation is prevalent. I do feel for them; I also want to have enough to care for myself too.

Clementine Neville

Cleveland, Ohio

February 26th, 2077.
